title: Wesfarmers recruits bot for productivity mission
full_text:
Wesfarmers is determined to embed artificial intelligence in its hardware, homewares and office supplies stores, its answer to broken promises over productivity reform that can’t come soon enough.
Its Bunnings chatbot running on Google’s Gemini model has handled more than 350,000 questions and gives DIY advice. At Kmart, the business is leaning on autonomous agents in sourcing, supply chain and store roles.
The pitch is part of a wider new productivity agenda from Wesfarmers chief executive Rob Scott, who is positioning AI to advance growth and counter an uncertain economic outlook where the cost of doing business is dulling earnings momentum.
Unveiling the conglomerate’s full-year results on Thursday, Mr Scott said there were many areas where AI was adding immediate value to the company, especially in terms of customer interaction with bots such as “Buddy” that translate into sales and put more items in baskets.
“We are seeing the conversion rates two to three times higher, we are seeing the average order value across whether it’s Bunnings, Kmart or Officeworks, anywhere from 20 per cent to 40 per cent higher, we are seeing deeper engagement with customers,” he said. “So when you allow for the additional sales we are generating that more offsets the additional costs associated with that system.” Wesfarmers warned a range of economic and public policy constraints is placing pressure on both consumers and businesses.
Mr Scott said the Albanese government’s clampdown on negative gearing and capital gains tax “haven’t done anything” to tackle the obvious problem of housing supply. All the budget measures have been aimed at curbing demand, but that doesn’t change complex and longer-term pressures pushing up prices.
“If you diagnose the fundamental problem with the housing market, what is making housing too expensive and not accessible, it’s a supply-side problem,” Mr Scott said. “Addressing the supply-side problem in housing is difficult because it requires co-operation across all levels of government – local, state, federal.
“It requires the right tax settings, and obviously we need to look at new and more innovative ways to address construction productivity. So it’s a complex issue.” Mr Scott called out the NSW and West Australian governments as trying to ease planning hurdles to get more houses built, with Wesfarmers recently inking a 50:50 joint venture with Built Group to establish Built Living, dedicated to delivering residential apartments at scale, which is also being supported by the federal National Reconstruction Fund.
Wesfarmers on Thursday reported annual sales increased 3.4 per cent to $47.27bn as net profit dipped 1.8 per cent to $2.87bn.
Net profit excluding significant items – which includes $279m from the gain on selling Coregas and profit from property sales – rose 8.3 per cent.
The earnings were in line with market expectations. Wesfarmers declared a final dividend of $1.20 per share, up from $1.11, payable on October 7. The stock fell 4.6 per cent to $79.47.
“Our businesses focused on mitigating cost pressures through productivity initiatives and were able to deliver more value, better service and increased convenience for our retail and business customers,” Mr Scott said.
“As households continued to experience cost-of-living pressures, our retail businesses dropped prices on thousands of products during the year to support household budgets.” Despite the slowdown in the housing market, Bunnings again reported strong growth, with sales up 4.1 per cent to $20.4bn and earnings better by 5.1 per cent at $2.46bn. Sales growth was observed across both consumer and commercial customers, and all product categories and regions.
That demand came from home improvement, repairs and maintenance, and a broader offering in tools, automotive, rural, pet and lifestyle categories.
Bunnings is also harnessing the power of AI through a team chatbot that Mr Scott believes has saved about 500,000 hours as staff in store are spending less time on administrative tasks and more time with customers.
The company also announced long-serving Bunnings boss Michael Schneider had signalled his intention to retire early next year, to be succeeded by Rachael McVitty, currently Bunnings’ chief customer officer.
At Kmart Group, which also owns Target, revenue increased 2.8 per cent to $11.75bn for the 2026 financial year. Earnings of $1.1bn were 6 per cent higher. Kmart Group continued to benefit from its strong value bias, Wesfarmers said, with customer numbers and transaction volumes growing on the prior year.
Prices were dropped on more than 2500 items during the year. At Officeworks, which is undergoing a restructure that has included job losses, sales rose 3.7 per cent to $3.7bn but earnings fell 20.3 per cent to $184m.
Its newest division, Wesfarmers Health, which operates Priceline pharmacies, skin clinics and other pharmaceutical and health operations, saw sales rise 9.1 per cent to $6.474bn as earnings lifted 18.8 per cent to $76m. Retail sales growth was supported by network expansion, a positive customer response to differentiated beauty, skincare and private label ranges and competitive pricing on more key value lines, Wesfarmers said.
Wesfarmers said that for the first seven weeks of the 2027 financial year, Bunnings’ sales growth was slightly stronger compared to the second half of the 2026 financial year, assisted by unseasonably dry weather in July. Kmart Group’s sales growth was in line with the same period. And Officeworks clung to growth, but that was slightly below the second half of 2026. “Uncertainty regarding ... inflation, house prices, interest rates and tax settings are affecting consumer sentiment, while higher costs of doing business are weighing on business confidence and spending,” Wesfarmers said.
